questions.q: Which chapter's idea is directly responsible for meridian-app1 getting an IAM role in Lesson 30 instead of a hardcoded access key?
options: Chapter 6 — CloudWatch monitoring
Chapter 7 — cost management
Chapter 3 — S3 and EBS storage
Chapter 1 — favor roles over long-lived access keys and give every workload its own identity
questions.explain: Chapter 1's core lesson on roles beating long-lived keys is exactly what Lesson 30 applied to meridian-app1.

questions.q: Why did Lesson 29 use t3.micro instances and a plain S3 bucket instead of the largest options available?
options: Larger instance types cannot be placed in a private subnet
t3.micro is the only instance type AWS offers in a VPC
S3 storage classes above the default are not available to new accounts
Right-sizing means matching the instance type and storage tier to the actual workload, not defaulting to the biggest option
questions.explain: Chapter 7's right-sizing argument is exactly what Lesson 29's modest, workload-matched choices demonstrate in practice.

questions.q: What two chapters' ideas combine to make meridian-app-sg allow traffic only from meridian-web-sg?
options: Chapter 1's IAM policies and Chapter 7's cost tagging
Chapter 2's AMI selection and Chapter 6's CloudWatch alarms
Chapter 3's S3 bucket policies and Chapter 5's CLI scripting
Chapter 4's subnetting and its security-group-to-security-group reference rules
questions.explain: Both the subnet split and the security-group reference rule used to scope traffic to the app tier come from Chapter 4's networking content.

questions.q: According to this capstone, what was Chapter 5's real purpose in this course?
options: A chapter students could safely skip since the console covers the same ground
A replacement for IAM roles and security groups
Only useful for Lesson 31's troubleshooting, with no relevance elsewhere
Not a standalone topic, but the thread that made every other chapter's commands legible and runnable
questions.explain: Nearly every command used across Chapters 1-7 and the capstone itself was an aws CLI call — Chapter 5 is what made all of them readable.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between an environment that is 'deployed' versus one that is 'administered,' as this capstone describes it?
options: An administered environment has monitoring, auditing, and cost alerts in place; a deployed one was simply stood up and left alone
A deployed environment always costs more than an administered one
There is no practical difference between the two terms
An administered environment uses only the AWS console, never the CLI
questions.explain: Chapters 6 and 7's CloudWatch alarms, CloudTrail logging, and Budget alerts are what turn a stood-up environment into one that's actually being watched and managed.
